summary: Cast-iron pierhead light at Kenosha, Wisconsin, built 1906; NRHP gives first light 1907, LighthouseFriends 1906; Board reports record 1891-1901 storm damage; sold at a 2011 auction; now automated.

lens.where: U.S. Coast Guard Station at Kenosha (NRHP)

structures.note: 50 ft (NRHP); NRHP says first lighted 1907; LighthouseFriends dates the fourth-order lens and flashing white light to 24 May 1906

structures.type: north pier, built by the Corps of Engineers
structures.note: Rehabilitated by the Corps 1969-1970 (NRHP); the pier is not original to the 1906 period

staffing.note: NRHP (2008): aids entirely automated; the date of automation is not given.

access.note: Accessible on foot by the north pier from Simmons Island Park (NRHP). The record says 'private'.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard in 2008 (NRHP); sold at a 2011 auction; Heather McGee later called owner (LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Federal government built a lighthouse on shore to mark the harbor, named Southport Light (NRHP).
Congress authorized $12,500 for harbor improvements (NRHP).
Wooden beacon, 12 ft high, at the outer end of the north pier (LighthouseFriends). NRHP dates the first pier beacon to 1856.
12-foot timber beacon on the north pier with a sixth-order lens, visible 9 miles (NRHP).
New taller wooden beacon on the north pier with a fixed red sixth-order lens, focal plane 30 ft (NRHP; LighthouseFriends).
Pierhead light moved 320 ft east to the end of the extended pier (LighthouseFriends).
Schooner Evaline ran into the pierhead light on 20 November 1891; watchroom damaged (Lighthouse Board report; LighthouseFriends).
Schooner entering the harbor in a gale on 25 November 1893 slightly damaged the rear beacon; repaired (Lighthouse Board report).
Conduit 104 ft long fitted to the pierhead light, installed 1893-94 (Lighthouse Board report; LighthouseFriends).
Gale on 1 November 1899 carried away the pierhead light and conduit. Relight given as 5 November in one entry and 'five days later' in another.
Sixth-order light moved about 380 ft east and 70 ft north to the outer end of the rebuilt pier (Lighthouse Board report for fiscal 1901).
Cast-iron tower erected at the end of a 750-foot pier (NRHP).
Present tower first lighted, with the fourth-order lens moved from the old Southport light on shore (NRHP). The record gives 1906; LighthouseFriends gives 24 May 1906 for the lens change.
Lens electrified; pierhead fog signal changed to an air diaphone (NRHP; LighthouseFriends).
Fourth-order lens removed in the 1960s and replaced by a modern beacon; lens on display at the Coast Guard station at Kenosha (NRHP).
Storm in the early 1980s severely damaged the cast-iron elevated walkway, which was dismantled (NRHP).
Vandals broke into the first story through a port-light, which was then sealed (NRHP).
VM-100 fog detector installed on the lantern gallery (NRHP).
Coast Guard deemed the light excess and offered it at no cost in June 2008 (LighthouseFriends).
Light placed on the General Services Administration auction website on 18 October 2010; minimum bid of $10,000 not received before the auction closed on 2 December (LighthouseFriends).
Second auction closed 15 July 2011 with a winning bid of $17,000 from John Burhani, a local artist (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Different structures are being compared: the 1842 shore light (Southport Light); the first pierhead beacon, dated 1848 by LighthouseFriends and 1856 by the NRHP; the 1867 wooden beacon; and the present tower, built 1906 and first lighted 1907. The record's 1856 refers to the first pierhead beacon, and 1906 to the present tower's construction.

resolved_conflicts.field: Sources differ on whether the light is still lit.
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 2008 nomination says the aids are entirely automated and that the light continues to guide vessels, so the light is still active.

resolved_conflicts.field: Sources differ by more than 3 m.
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The heights compared are of different structures: a 12-ft (3.7 m) beacon, a 30-ft (9.1 m) wooden beacon, and the 50-ft (15.2 m) present tower.

The NRHP says the fourth-order lens was installed in the new pierhead light, 'which was first lighted in 1907'. LighthouseFriends dates the change from a sixth-order fixed red light to a fourth-order flashing white light, with the Kenosha Lighthouse lens, to 24 May 1906. The record gives 1906. The sources disagree and the story states both dates.

The record's claim that a light has marked the harbour since 1842 is not used. LighthouseFriends describes the 1861 list as showing the pierhead beacon no longer lighted after the sea carried it away, and a temporary beacon blown down by 1860. The story gives 1842 only as the year the federal government built a lighthouse on shore.

notes_for_editor: Roster matched by name (USLHS position 0.2 km from the station's). First-light dispute: NRHP gives 1856 for a 12-ft timber beacon with a sixth-order lens; LighthouseFriends gives 1848 for a 12-ft wooden beacon. No Lighthouse Board volume before 1891 is in the local corpus, so the dispute is not settled. Present tower: NRHP says first lighted 1907; LighthouseFriends dates the lens and flashing white light change to 24 May 1906; the record says 1906. Both dates are in the story and no correction is proposed, because the sources disagree. A Chronicling America search for Kenosha pierhead, Wisconsin, 1906-1907 found nothing, so the 1907 date rests on the NRHP alone. Record range_nm 6.9 against the NRHP's 'visible for 12 miles in clear weather' (units unstated; not changed). Record other_names holds the placeholder 'ADD Name' and a 'Kenosha South Pier Light' that was not checked. Record access 'private' against the NRHP's 'accessible on foot'. Ownership: the NRHP describes Coast Guard ownership, undated in its text. LighthouseFriends reports the Coast Guard offered the light at no cost in June 2008; a GSA auction from 18 October 2010 drew no bid of at least $10,000; and a second auction closed 15 July 2011 at $17,000 to John Burhani, a local artist. It later names Heather McGee as owner. The story gives those public facts only. Personal details LighthouseFriends prints about the buyer (illness, death, childhood) are deliberately left out, under the living-people rule. The 1899 relight date is internally inconsistent in the 1900 report (5 November in one entry; 'five days later' in another). Lighthouse Board OCR text was read as text, not by column. Printed page numbers for scan 483 (p. 142) are read from the page header; scan 482's printed page is unconfirmed, so it is cited by scan page only. Several Life-Saving Service Kenosha Station rescues in the 1880s appear in the corpus near the harbor piers; no source read ties them to this light, so they are not in the record. The archive lists 'Anton J. DePrang' (1906) and 'Anton De Frang' (1911) separately; they are not merged. The archive spells Louis N. De Diemar as one word in its page; LighthouseFriends uses 'DeDiemer'; the archive's spelling is kept.
